newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian army has $11 million debts. [CORRECTED 18:43 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian army has $11 million debts. [CORRECTED 18:43 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects headline to $11 million from $10 million to conform with the text.)

The armed forces of former Warsaw Pact member Bulgaria have run up debts of four billion levs ($11 million) to suppliers, mostly for food and uniforms, Defence Minister Dimitar Pavlov said on Tuesday.

"We are part of this country and if the whole country is in a state of economic crisis, I have to admit that the Bulgarian army is also experiencing the difficulties of this crisis," he told a news conference.
He said the debts, worth more than $11 million at Tuesday's exchange rate of the rapidly depreciating lev, were owed to private and state companies.

He said the armed forces could not depend on government cash to keep troops fed over the winter but would have to make their own arrangements. Many units have their own farms, which produce 86 percent of the meat consumed by troops.

The International Institute for Strategic Studies numbers Bulgaria's army at 51,600, its airforce at 21,600 and the navy at 3,000, including a total of 51,300 conscripts. There are also about 10,000 construction troops.

"We had discussions on the draft budget for 1997 and I should admit I am not happy with what was proposed by Bulgaria's finance minister, so we will concentrate our efforts to secure food and basic needs for our soldiers," Pavlov said.
Conscripts complain they get too much bean soup, but Pavlov denied newspaper reports that the army was feeding troops on dog or donkey meat.

Military service of 18 months is compulsory in Bulgaria. Conscripts are often allowed home at weekends so they can eat with their families, who complain they have to give them pocket money as their token wage barely buys three packets of cigarettes.
"I can assure you that throughout the winter our army will be able to secure the country's defence," Pavlov said.
Pavlov said the armed forces needed at least $20 billion over 10 years to modernise their equipment, which the state will be unable to provide.

The defence ministry is in contact with its Balkan neighbours Romania, Greece and Turkey, and also Russia and other countries through NATO's Partnership for Peace programme, which encourages links between NATO's 16 members, former Warsaw Pact countries and neutral European states.
Bulgaria's anti-communist opposition is keen to bring the Balkan country into NATO but the ruling Socialists want to avoid upsetting their Russian allies.
President-elect Petar Stoyanov, who takes office in January, has pledged to bring the country closer to the Atlantic alliance. ($1=360.86 Leva)
